content:
Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said she “genuinely believes” Vice President JD Vance’s indecision about running for president in 2028, suggesting that being a present father is contributing to the difficulty.

“I’ve had the pleasure of getting to know the vice president, his lovely wife, Usha. I’ve spent a lot of time with them and their children, and one thing I learned in becoming friends with them is that the vice president really does make an effort to be a very present father,” Leavitt told Fox News’ Ainsley Earhardt on Tuesday morning.

“That’s obviously very difficult as the vice president of the United States. It would be even more difficult, if not impossible, when running a presidential campaign,” she continued. “So I believe him when he says he’s still grappling with the decision.”

The vice president appeared on the network the day before for an interview with host Laura Ingraham, where he stated he has yet to decide on running. His stance comes after his party’s brutal defeat in the midterm elections that many attribute to the administration’s handling of key issues.

Vance told Ingraham he “will be all-in on whatever that decision is,” but Earhardt on Tuesday said a White House source told the network “he will most likely throw his hat in the race.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who also has children, is also among those considered likely to enter the 2028 presidential race.

Earhardt noted a recent interview in which Vance said his wife “really doesn’t like politics,” adding that she wonders “if that will play into his decision.”

“Is it now or never for him?” she asked the former press secretary. “What if he says, ‘I’m going to wait a while till my children grow up, and then I’ll make a decision.’ Or does he have to decide now? Is this his time?”

Leavitt, who President Donald Trump said resigned from her role so “she can spend more time with her beautiful young children and family,” told Earhardt, “You really never know what’s going to happen.”

“If 2028 is not the year for him, who knows what this country will look like four years later? What new candidates, who we don’t even know about right now, will emerge?” Leavitt said.
